2.text: Knives were drawn and they threatened to cut the sinews of the legs

3.text: of the offender, that he might not be able to kick again. Nevertheless

4.text: they did not come to blows. A few days afterwards, when the passions of

5.text: both parties had cooled down, the young man who was threatened declared

6.text: that he was in the right when he wrenched the piece of wood from his as-

7.text: sailant and kicked him; and he therefore wanted to have reparation for the

8.text: unsheathing of iron in his camp. Finally he was actually given as kɪˊtkau

9.text: (“hard return,” i. e., reparation, see p. 669) a set of reindeer leg-skins. The

10.text: value of the gift was insignificant, and it had chiefly a moral effect.

11.text: Shortly after my first arrival at the Anui fair, I had a visit from Eiˊheli,

12.text: Qituˊwg̣i, and other chiefs of the Chukchee. They bade me welcome in a

13.text: manner rather ceremonial, but they were really wishing for a drink of brandy

14.text: as a token of welcome on my part, which they accordingly received. There

15.text: were five or six of them. Then more people came and asked for the same,

16.text: and at last I stopped the supply. One of the later comers, who had had

17.text: nothing, insisted also on having a sip of the liquor. Soon he became so im-

18.text: portunate, that I lost patience and asked him to leave me in peace. He sat

19.text: down in his place, grumbling to himself. A couple of hours afterwards I

20.text: was standing in the gate of the fortress, talking with the people who were

21.text: passing to and fro, and making occasional notes in a little note-book that I

22.text: held in my hands. Suddenly my recent guest came up from behind and struck

23.text: me with his fist on my right wrist, so that my note-book fell to the ground.

24.text: “You so and so!” cried he, “you come here and hobnob with the people for

25.text: hours and scribble notes on a paper, but one cannot get a draught of brandy

26.text: in your blessed house.” After that he retreated a little, stripped off his fur

27.text: shirt, and was quite naked down to his waist. Then he requested me to do

28.text: the same, and to have a wrestling-match with him. “I am standing on my

29.text: own ground,” added he, “and I may challenge you to a test.” He was right,

30.text: in so far as even officially only the interior of the fortress was considered to

31.text: be Russian territory, and all the space outside of it was admitted to belong

32.text: to the Chukchee. Every evening all the Chukchee were turned out of the

33.text: fortress and the gate locked, so that the difference was more than theoretical.

34.text: A young boy of about ten years kept tugging at the clothes of this man with

35.text: all his might, trying to persuade him to be off to the house. This was his

36.text: son. But the father was firm in his intention. My adversary was a man of

37.text: fifty, of Maritime extraction, Rɪˊnto by name. He was of slender frame, but

38.text: his temper was undaunted. As a result of this, he had two ugly scars in

39.text: the region of his abdomen. I felt no desire, however, for the unexpected

40.text: wrestling-match. At the same time I. did not like the idea of openly retreating

41.text: before my adversary, though he stood on his own territory, and I stood on

42.text: mine. The difficulty resolved itself, however, by the arrival of one of my

43.text: friends, a political exile like myself, who was a man of powerful build and
